summary: Defines the profile for Route Origin Authorizations. A ROA is a signed object proving that the holder of an address block has authorized a particular AS to originate routes for prefixes in that block. It is a standards-track document that was replaced by RFC 9582.

plainLanguage.summary: A Route Origin Authorization, or ROA, is a signed record that says a particular network is allowed to announce routes for a block of IP addresses. A network that checks ROAs can tell whether an announcement came from the address holder or from someone else. This document defines the exact format of that record.

questions: what is maxlength in a roa
subtitle: A signed record that says one network is allowed to announce routes for a block of IP addresses.

tldr.problem: Routing on the Internet relies on an Autonomous System announcing the addresses it is entitled to originate. Anyone can announce any prefix, so there is no way to check whether a given announcement was authorized by the holder of the address space.
tldr.mechanism: A Route Origin Authorization is a digitally signed object that names one Autonomous System and the prefixes it is allowed to originate. It uses the RPKI signed object template, with the content encoded in ASN.1, and a validator checks the signature and the address delegation extension of the certificate inside it.
tldr.outcome: A relying party can decide whether a route announcement is covered by an authorization, which is what the RPKI routing security system is built on. The profile has been replaced by RFC 9582.

facts.label: Maximum prefix length
facts.value: 32 bits for IPv4, 128 bits for IPv6

facts.label: Encoding of the eContent
facts.value: ASN.1 with the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER)

today: RFC 6482 was a Proposed Standard published in February 2012. It has been obsoleted by RFC 9582, which is the current profile for Route Origin Authorizations.

sections.title: Why Route Origin Authorizations Exist
sections.content:
The primary purpose of the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) is to improve routing security. Part of that system is a mechanism that lets entities verify that an Autonomous System (AS) has been given permission by an IP address block holder to advertise routes to one or more prefixes within that block. A ROA provides this function.

The ROA uses the template for RPKI digitally signed objects, which defines a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) wrapper for the ROA content as well as a generic validation procedure for RPKI signed objects. To complete the specification of the ROA, this document defines three things: the OID that identifies the signed object as being a ROA, the ASN.1 syntax for the ROA eContent, and the additional validation step that a ROA needs on top of the generic RPKI checks.

The OID appears in the eContentType of the encapContentInfo object and in the content-type signed attribute of the signerInfo object. The eContent is the payload that names the AS being authorized to originate routes and the prefixes it may originate routes for, and it is ASN.1 encoded using the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER).

The content of a ROA identifies a single AS that the address space holder has authorized to originate routes, together with a list of one or more IP address prefixes that will be advertised. If the holder needs to authorize several ASes for the same prefixes, the holder issues multiple ROAs, one per AS number.
sections.plainLanguage: A ROA is a signed statement that one network may announce routes for a set of IP addresses. A network that holds the addresses signs it, and anyone who can read the ROA can check who was given the right to announce what.

sections.title: The ASN.1 Structure of a ROA
sections.content:
The content type for a ROA is defined as routeOriginAuthz and has the numerical value 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.24. This OID MUST appear both within the eContentType in the encapContentInfo object and the content-type signed attribute in the signerInfo object.

The eContent is a RouteOriginAttestation, a sequence of a version, an asID and a sequence of ipAddrBlocks. The version number MUST be 0. The asID field contains the AS number that is authorized to originate routes to the given IP address prefixes. The ipAddrBlocks field encodes the set of IP address prefixes to which the AS is authorized to originate routes.

Each entry of ipAddrBlocks is a ROAIPAddressFamily, holding an addressFamily octet string of two or three bytes and a sequence of ROAIPAddress structures. Each of those holds an address, which is an IP address given as a bit string, and an optional maxLength. The syntax is more restrictive than the IP address delegation extension: that extension can represent arbitrary address ranges, whereas ROAs need to represent only prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: A ROA has three parts: a version number that must be 0, the AS number that is allowed to announce, and the list of address prefixes. Inside the list, each address family holds prefixes with an optional limit on how long those prefixes may be.

sections.title: Prefixes and Maximum Length
sections.content:
The addressFamily field contains the Address Family Identifier (AFI) of an IP address family. This specification supports only IPv4 and IPv6, so addressFamily MUST be either 0001 or 0002.

The addresses field represents prefixes as a sequence of type IPAddress. If present, the maxLength MUST be an integer greater than or equal to the length of the accompanying prefix, and less than or equal to the length in bits of an IP address in the address family: 32 for IPv4 and 128 for IPv6. When present, maxLength specifies the maximum length of the IP address prefix that the AS is authorized to advertise.

The RFC works through an example. If the IP address prefix is 203.0.113/24 and the maxLength is 26, the AS is authorized to advertise any more specific prefix with a maximum length of 26. In that example the AS would be authorized to advertise 203.0.113/24, 203.0.113.128/25 or 203.0.113.0/25, but not 203.0.113.0/27. When maxLength is not present, the AS is only authorized to advertise the exact prefix specified in the ROA.

A valid ROA may contain a prefix that is encompassed by another prefix in a separate ROAIPAddress element. A ROA may contain the prefix 203.0.113/24 with maxLength 26 as well as the prefix 203.0.113.0/28 with maxLength 28, which would authorize the AS to advertise any prefix beginning with 203.0.113 with a minimum length of 24 and a maximum length of 26, as well as the specific prefix 203.0.113.0/28. A ROA MAY contain two ROAIPAddress elements with an identical prefix, but this is NOT RECOMMENDED, because the element with the shorter maxLength grants no additional privileges and can be omitted without changing the meaning of the ROA.
sections.plainLanguage: Without a maximum length, the ROA authorizes exactly one prefix. With one, it authorizes that prefix and any longer prefix down to the limit given. The RFC uses 203.0.113/24 with a limit of 26 to show this: a /24 and two /25s are allowed, but a /27 is not.

sections.title: ROA Validation
sections.content:
Before a relying party can use a ROA to validate a routing announcement, the relying party MUST first validate the ROA. To validate a ROA, the relying party MUST perform all the validation checks specified by the RPKI signed object profile as well as the following additional ROA-specific validation step: the IP address delegation extension must be present in the end-entity (EE) certificate contained within the ROA, and each IP address prefix in the ROA must be contained within the set of IP addresses specified by the EE certificate's IP address delegation extension.

In other words, the certificate that travels with the ROA has to cover the prefixes the ROA names. If the end-entity certificate does not hold the address space, the ROA grants nothing.
sections.plainLanguage: To use a ROA, a validator first checks the signature and the rest of the RPKI checks, then confirms that the certificate inside the ROA really covers the prefixes the ROA lists. A ROA that names addresses its certificate does not hold is not valid.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There is no assumption of confidentiality for the data in a ROA. It is anticipated that ROAs will be stored in repositories that are accessible to all ISPs, and perhaps to all Internet users. There is no explicit authentication associated with a ROA, since the PKI used for ROA validation provides authorization but not authentication. Although the ROA is a signed, application-layer object, there is no intent to convey non-repudiation via a ROA.

The purpose of a ROA is to convey authorization for an AS to originate a route to the prefixes in the ROA, so the integrity of a ROA MUST be established. The ROA uses the RPKI signed object format, so all the security considerations of that profile apply to ROAs, and the signed object profile uses the CMS signed message format for integrity, so ROAs inherit all the security considerations associated with that data structure.

The right of the ROA signer to authorize the target AS to originate routes to the prefixes is established through the address space and AS number PKI. Specifically, one MUST verify the signature on the ROA using an X.509 certificate issued under this PKI, and check that the prefixes in the ROA match those in the certificate's address space extension.
sections.plainLanguage: A ROA is not secret. It is meant to be published so that anyone can check it. Its value comes from its integrity, so the signature must be verified against a certificate issued by the address space and AS number PKI.

viz.caption: THE FIELDS OF THE ROA eContent

items.title: version
items.text: The version number of the RouteOriginAttestation, which MUST be 0.

items.title: asID
items.text: The AS number authorized to originate routes to the given prefixes.

items.title: ipAddrBlocks
items.text: The set of IP address prefixes the AS may originate routes to.

items.title: addressFamily
items.text: The Address Family Identifier: 0001 for IPv4 or 0002 for IPv6.

items.title: addresses
items.text: A sequence of ROAIPAddress structures, one per prefix.

items.title: maxLength
items.text: Optional. The longest prefix the AS may advertise, at most 32 bits for IPv4 and 128 for IPv6.
